In brief The collaborative multi-agent and robot system (MARS), a hierarchical knowledge-driven framework coordinating 19 LLM agents with 16 domain-specific tools, is developed to accelerate materials research. By coordinating specialized agents with domain-specific tools, MARS autonomously exec

utes full-cycle materials development, from design to synthesis and optimization. The system demonstrated a 60-fold acceleration in developing a water-stable perovskite nanocomposite through cross-domain knowledge integration. This paradigm shift enables researchers to focus on creative problem-solving while AI handles repetitive tasks, fundamentally changing materials innovation approaches. tion, the system PROGRESS AND POTENTIAL Large language models (LLMs) provide new possibilities for accelerating ma￾terials research, yet their application in complex materials science remains limited. Here, we developed the collaborative multi-agent and robot system (MARS), a knowledge-driven hierarchical architecture coordi￾nating 19 LLM agents with 16 domain-specific tools organized into functional modules, achieving closed￾loop autonomous materials discovery by integrating robotic experimentation. MARS offers accurate and pro￾fessional guidance for materials development and relieves the hallucination inherent to current LLMs through a hybrid retrieval-augmented generation approach. As experimental validation, the system demonstrates its capabilities in perovskite nanocrystal development, optimizing synthesis protocols within 10 experimental iterations and designing a biomimetic ‘‘core

-shell-corona’’ structure for water-stable perovskite composites within 3.5 h compared to conventional methods requiring 4–6 months. Through an interactive natural lan￾guage interface, researchers can orchestrate experiments while tracking real-time agent coordination. Beyond efficiency gains, MARS represents a paradigm shift toward truly autonomous materials research where knowledge-driven AI can initiate scientific discovery. MARS can combine knowledge from different scientific fields to create solutions that human researchers might overlook, as demonstrated by its biomi￾metic design inspired by cell membranes. Looking forward, we envision MARS accelerating discoveries across critical areas including renewable energy materials, medical compounds, and sustainable technolo￾gies. This could help address urgent global challenges like climate change and healthcare needs by removing research

bottlenecks. As the system evolves, it could democratize advanced materials research by reducing dependence on specialized infrastructure and expertise, allowing scientists worldwide to focus on creative problem-solving rather than repetitive tasks. MARS represents not just an improvement in research effi￾ciency but also a fundamental shift in how we approach materials innovation. This acceleration automates literature review and experimental planning, allowing re￾searchers to focus on creative thinking while interacting through a natural language interface. This work establishes an integrated AI-driven framework for accelerating materials innovation and presents a paradigm for AI-enabled scientific discovery. INTRODUCTION Materials are the foundation of human understanding and trans￾formation of the world, and innovations in this field are critical to societal progress and technological advancement.1,2 The dis￾covery and application of new materials is typically a complex, lengthy, and costly process that requires the accumulation of multidiscipli

nary knowledge, extensive study of prior research, expertise in preparation techniques, time-intensive experimental iterations, and thorough validation in practical scenarios.3–6 To enhance the efficiency of materials innovation, scientists have made sustained and long-term efforts, such as the launch of the Materials Genome Initiative in 2011, which aims to accelerate materials discovery using high-throughput computational and experimental platforms.7–9 Despite these advances, the devel￾opment of new materials typically still requires years, highlighting the urgent need for new methodologies to accelerate the pace of materials research. Since OpenAI released ChatGPT, large language models (LLMs) have attracted widespread research interest, leading to substantial breakthroughs across various fields.10,11 LLMs can serve as invaluable research assistants and aid researchers in effi￾ciently

mining literature, quickly accessing critical data, and providing potential optimization strategies.12–15 Besides, LLMs have recently shown exceptional abilities in code generation, specialized tool integration, and strategic planning.16–23These ad￾vances have enabled several pioneering studies that successfully couple LLM-powered agents with robotic experimentation plat￾forms, achieving autonomous chemical synthesis,24,25 acceler￾ated reaction optimization,26 and intelligent synthesis route recommendation,27 thereby demonstrating the transformative potential of AI-driven laboratory automation. These capabilities are particularly valuable for materials science, where the inher￾ently multidisciplinary nature demands precise knowledge extrac￾tion and integration from an ever-expanding scientific literature.28 This is particularly evident in nanomaterials research, a field char￾acterized b

y an explosion of scientific literature over the past two decades, yet struggles with challenges of research redundancy and reproducibility.29,30 While promising, leveraging the full potential of LLMs for autonomous materials research requires ad￾dressing key challenges, including accurate comprehension of domain-specific knowledge, mitigation of hallucinations, robust control of automated synthesis, efficient management of complex tasks, and development of systematic workflows. Herein, we develop a knowledge-driven multi-agent and robot system (MARS) for end-to-end autonomous materials discovery. MARS employs a collaborative network of 19 specialized LLM agents with access to 16 domain-specific tools to orchestrate complex material research tasks by integrating the robotic plat￾form. Critically, MARS leverages a comprehensive materials sci￾ence knowledge base that guides its reasoning a

nd mitigates hallucinations, providing professional guidance and designing multi-step synthesis processes compatible with automated ro￾botic platforms. Subsequently, MARS can control multiple ro￾botic platforms to autonomously execute iterative experiments (synthesis, analysis, and optimization) to achieve research ob￾jectives, demonstrated by successfully tuning green-emitting perovskite nanocrystals to target blue emission within 10 exper￾imental iterations. These capabilities enable MARS to function as a human research team with superior domain-specific expertise compared to existing LLM-based systems. Furthermore, demonstrating its accelerated discovery potential, MARS auton￾omously designed and synthesized CsPbBr3@LP/PEG compos￾ite with enhanced water stability and biocompatibility within 3.5 h, significantly accelerating materials development by 60-fold compared with the traditiona

l method. By automating literature review, experimental planning, and protocol optimization, MARS allows human researchers to redirect their focus toward higher-level scientific insights, hypothesis generation, and crea￾tive problem-solving. Moreover, a user-friendly web interface fa￾cilitates intuitive interaction with MARS, enabling researchers to specify research objectives in natural language and monitor the automated workflow, creating a synergistic human-AI partner￾ship that maximizes scientific productivity and accelerates the pace of materials innovation. RESULTS The architecture of MARS This automated materials research framework employs a multi￾agent system architecture that is analogous to a well-coordi￾nated research laboratory. The MARS framework coordinates a network of 19 specialized agents, enabling complex multi￾objective tasks in materials design, synthesis, and analysi

s through collaborative intelligence. These agents constitute a higher-level framework built on LLMs, leveraging their core reasoning and generative capabilities while incorporating task definition, dynamic utilization of 16 professional toolkits, and feedback loops to achieve complex objectives beyond the ca￾pacity of standalone LLMs. As shown in Figure 1A, the system is hierarchically structured into five synergistic functional groups with distinct responsibilities to emulate the real-world scientific research team, including the ORCHESTRATOR group (G1), SCIENTIST group (G2), ENGINEER group (G3), EXECUTOR group (G4), and ANALYST group (G5) (see Note S1). The ORCHESTRATOR Group serves as the central coordi￾nator, plans sub-tasks based on user requests, and selects the appropriate agent group to complete the sub-task, while 2 Matter 9, 102577, February 4, 2026 Article ll

managing the message queue between agent groups. The SCIENTIST group, equipped with the hybrid retrieval￾augmented generation (RAG) strategy and several customized information retrieval tools, focuses on materials knowledge retrieval and solution design, satisfying materials synthesis, structure, property, and application requirements. The ENGINEER group translates scientific proposals into executable protocols, bridging the gap between theoretical design and practical implementation. As presented in Figure 1B, the EXECUTOR group interacts with automated experimental plat￾forms to carry out these protocols, controlling instrumentation, collecting data, and ensuring the reliable execution of designed experiments. Finally, the ANALYST Group analyzes experi￾mental results and generates refinement strategies, driving iter￾ative improvement and optimization based on experimental data. This mo

dular design allows for specialized expertise and efficient task distribution among the agent groups.31 An effective, hierarchical message-passing mechanism is crucial to MARS, enabling multimodal (text, code, data, and im￾age) communication between and within functional groups. Similar to information flow in research laboratories, the ORCHESTRATOR (G1) acts as a central hub, receiving user re￾quests, analyzing requirements, planning, and distributing sub￾tasks to administrator agents (function as team leaders) within each group (G2–G5). These administrator agents further hand off sub-tasks to specialized agents within their respective groups. Leveraging domain expertise and dedicated tools (e.g., GraphRAG for SCIENTIST, Python REPL for ENGINEER, and Matplotlib for ANALYST), these agents execute their as￾signed tasks. Results are aggregated by the administrators and returned to the ORCHE

STRATOR, which evaluates them and adjusts the whole sub-task list, assigning tasks or returning final results. This hierarchical structure, with clearly defined roles and communication pathways, ensures efficient collaboration, robust task management, and a streamlined, adaptable work￾flow for materials design. As illustrated in Figure 1C, MARS integrates a human-in-the￾loop mechanism, enabling dynamic task adjustment and optimi￾zation through user interaction and feedback with the ORCHESTRATOR. This allows expert intervention and validation at critical decision points when agents request assistance from experts, effectively combining computational efficiency with hu￾man expertise to ensure practical validity while maintaining autonomous operation. Figure 1D presents the user-friendly interface that facilitates user interaction and real-time monitoring of the experimental workflow (see N

ote S2 and Figures S1 and S2). As shown in Figure 1E, the capabilities of MARS have been validated by designing and synthesizing Figure 1. Architecture of MARS (A) Overview of the MARS system. Knowledge-driven automated experimentation Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances language model outputs by incorporating relevant information from external knowledge sources before generating responses. This approach grounds model outputs in factual, domain-specific in￾formation, thereby reducing hallucinations that commonly occur when models rely exclusively on knowledge embedded during training.32 MARS integrates materials knowledge retrieval with experimental execution, forming complementary cognitive and physical dimensions that enable the system to transition from conceptual understanding to real-world synthesis. Research on materials typically begins with comprehensive literature re￾view and information retrieval. The SCIENTIST group acceler￾ates this process through a hybrid RAG approa

ch that trans￾forms unstructured scientific literature into structured experimental guidance. Our hybrid RAG framework combines traditional vector similarity search with graph-based retrieval methods (GraphRAG), enabling more comprehensive and con￾textually aware information retrieval for complex materials sci￾ence queries. As illustrated in Figure 2A, four specialized LLM-based agents within the SCIENTIST group focus on distinct areas: structure, synthesis, properties, and applications, each contributing distinct expertise while leveraging specialized retrieval tools. The core retrieval system combines three primary approaches: KeywordSearch for word-level query matching, VectorSearch for semantic-level similarity-based matching, and GraphRAG for topic-level view through the knowledge graph. This hybrid approach ensures comprehensive query results by balancing sentence matching, paragra

ph matching, and topic view. As shown in Figure 2B, MARS utilizes an extensive knowledge base carefully constructed from academic papers, books, and web resources to support this retrieval system (see Note S3). These diverse sources are converted to markdown format for natural segmentation and then enhanced with vector represen￾tations for similarity searches and structured into knowledge graphs for conceptual reasoning.33–35 Online resources (WebSearch, LitSearch, and DatabaseSearch) supplement the offline knowledge base when required. Upon receiving a sub￾task from the ORCHESTRATOR, the admin agent of the SCIENTIST group routes it to the most appropriate specialized agent using tailored prompts. These specialized agents utilize hybrid retrieval tools to acquire relevant domain knowledge when needed, thus enhancing the accuracy of their responses. To demonstrate the capabilities of MARS

, the synthesis of perovskite nanocubes is selected as a representative task. CsPbBr3 perovskites are promising for optoelectronic applica￾tions, but their nanocrystal synthesis is complex, with multiple interdependent factors including precursor selection, ligand en￾gineering, reaction temperature control, and precise timing of various steps. For this demonstration, a specialized knowledge base was constructed from 1,348 high-impact perovskite publi￾cations, resulting in a vector database (7,818 segments) and a comprehensive knowledge graph (117,749 nodes and 232,490 edges), which provides a rich foundation for material synthesis reasoning (see Figures S3 and S4). As shown in Figure 2C, MARS demonstrates superior performance by accurately retrieving precise reagent specifications and procedural details (see Note S4), whereas conventional LLMs like GPT-4o, o3- mini, and Llama 3.1-70B pro

duce hallucinations. Regarding hal￾lucinations, we identified several issues: numerical fabrication (such as providing integer values rather than stoichiometric ra￾tios), incorrect synthesis conditions (inappropriate solvent or precursor selection), omission of critical experimental steps, and disregard for user constraints (see Note S5). MARS miti￾gates these issues through its multi-agent RAG architecture and addresses the knowledge deficit, which is identified as the fundamental cause of hallucinations.36 As shown in Figure 2D, knowledge is transformed into action through the ENGINEER and EXECUTOR groups, which convert conceptual understanding into physical experimentation. Figure 2E illustrates the ENGINEER group, which serves as the crucial bridge, translating synthesis protocols into machine￾executable instructions through four specialized agents: the scheme plotter creates visual

flowcharts for human verification, the structural engineer converts protocols to standardized JSON schemas, the software engineer generates specialized code when needed,37,38 and the code reviewer ensures operational safety and feasibility (see Note S6). Subsequently, the EXECUTOR group implements these instructions through a self-developed experimental robotic platform5 (see Figure S5) that integrates workstation controller, mobile-robot controller, and characterization controller agents communicating with uni￾fied control middleware (see Figure S6). Figure 2F demonstrates this workflow through the automated room temperature synthesis of CsPbBr3 nanocrystals. Upon receiving the synthesis scheme from the SCIENTIST group, the ENGINEER group transforms the protocol into machine-execut￾able instructions, which are subsequently passed to the EXECUTOR group. The workstation and mobile-robot c

ontroller agents transmit these instructions through the scheme transmis￾sion API tool to the unified control middleware on the computer workstation, thereby initiating the physical synthesis process. The middleware coordinates a sequence of automated opera￾tions: (1) mobile robots locate reagents and consumables from storage areas (no. 1–3); (2) the robots transport reagent bottles to the adding device (no. 4–5); (3) the materials are transferred to the liquid workstation (no. 6) for precise pipetting, stirring, and heating; and (4) the completed samples are transported to the fluorescence spectrometer (no. 7) for characterization. Throughout this process, spectroscopic data are transmitted to the middleware and accessed by the DataCollector agent for analysis. Knowledge-driven automated experimentation Parameter optimization is a critical component in materials sci￾ence research. Conve

ntional machine learning methods generally require extensive experimental data to build optimization models, but data are lacking in actual experimental processes. Figure 3A illustrates how MARS implements a paradigm shift by employing knowledge-driven reasoning rather than relying on data-intensive modeling approaches. By leveraging the powerful reasoning ca￾pabilities of LLMs combined with comprehensive materials 4 Matter 9, 102577, February 4, 2026 Article ll

knowledge, the system can perform advanced parameter optimi￾zation and synthesis prediction with minimal experimental data.15 This paradigm shift enables efficient exploration of synthesis pa￾rameters without the high-throughput experimentation typically required by machine learning methods. The Experiment Optimizer agent demonstrates effective LLM specialization through struc￾tured system prompts. The prompt design includes several essential elements: clear role definition (‘‘You are a professional Experiment_Optimizer’’), integration with analytical tools (Scikit￾Learn, Optuna, and Matminer for modeling), and access to domain-specific literature through RAG retrieval and online search tools. This design implements a decision framework that directs the agent to select between code-based modeling for data-rich scenarios and knowledge-based parameter adjustment when data are limited, mimi

cking the actual workflow of materials scientists. Besides, the ANALYST_Admin agent enhances system robustness by providing critical coordination and quality control functions, including verification of chemical validity and Figure 2. As shown in Figure 3B, the capabilities of MARS in feedback￾driven optimization were demonstrated through the challenging task of tuning perovskite nanocrystal emission from green (523 nm) to blue (460 nm). All-inorganic perovskite nanocrystals have attracted considerable research interest due to their facile colloidal synthesis, tunable emission wavelengths spanning the entire visible spectrum, high photoluminescence quantum yields, and narrow emission bands. Wavelength tuning through halide composition engineering represents a crucial research di￾rection with significant applications in light-emitting diodes (LEDs), lasers, and quantum light sources. Besides, this task demonstrates a classic materials optimization

challenge that re￾quires precise control over quantum confinement effects and composition, typically achieved through halide exchange (Br to Cl substitution) or dimensional control. This optimization process demands professional reasoning about how precursor ratios and reaction conditions affect band-gap engineering in semicon￾ductor nanocrystals, guided by well-defined targets with quanti￾fiable outcomes. From an experimental demonstration perspec￾tive, this optimization task provides rapid visual feedback through color changes and enables real-time optical character￾ization, effectively highlighting the multi-parameter optimization capabilities of MARS. Figure 3C presents the distribution of key reagents (including solvents, Cs sources, Pb sources, and ligands) reported in the literature for room temperature antisolvent precipitation of blue-emitting perovskites. the MARS knowledge base to help researchers establish a chemically reasonable design space grounded in prior experi￾mental work. Notably, achieving the target 460 nm emission re￾mains a zero-shot optimization challenge that requires iterative reasoning through complex constraints without prior experi￾mental data for this specific target. Figure 3D shows the merit function, defined as the difference between the emission peak of the product and the target value, which is designed to assess optimization progress. For comparison, three parallel optimiza￾tion iterations using MARS, currently one of the most powerful closed-source LLMs (GPT-4o), and the leading open-source LLM (Mistral Large2) were performed. To ensure scientific rigor and fairness in our comparative evaluation, we designed a controlled experiment where all participating models (MARS, GPT-4o, and Mistral Large 2) received iden

tical standardized input formats. Notably, in preliminary tests requiring indepen￾dent synthesis protocol generation for 523 nm CsPbBr3 nano￾crystals (NCs) without any starting recipe, only MARS success￾fully provided a complete and executable ligand-assisted reprecipitation synthesis protocol. In contrast, GPT-4o and Mistral Large 2 could only provide vague guidance or even demonstrate fundamental chemical misconceptions, high￾lighting the professional knowledge gap between specialized and general-purpose models. All models began optimization from the same initial recipe (523 nm emission) provided by MARS for the formal optimization comparison. Optimization concluded upon reaching a merit value >0.95 or after 15 iterations. To ensure fair comparison, the optimization suggestions from GPT-4o and Mistral Large 2 were manually input into the automated experimental platform of MARS for exec

ution, as MARS functions as an integrated design-experiment-optimization system capable of directly executing synthesis protocols and obtaining experimental feed￾back, whereas other models only provide textual responses. Each model received identical iterative feedback in a standard￾ized table format containing current emission peak, historical data, and optimization targets (see Note S7). As presented in Figure 3E, MARS requires an average of only 8.3 iterations to reach the stopping condition, while GPT-4o and Mistral Large2 require 12.7 and 12.3 iterations, respectively. Mistral Large2 even fails to reason correctly once under the given rules, remain￾ing far from the target even after more than 15 iterations. Figure 3F demonstrates how MARS achieves the target within ten iterative optimization cycles, highlighting its capability to autonomously use domain knowledge for guiding subsequ

ent experimental decisions. This knowledge-driven approach significantly reduces the experimental burden by requiring fewer iterations to reach targets, allowing researchers to explore syn￾thesis parameters more efficiently than standalone LLMs. Supe￾rior optimization efficiency in the MARS system is achieved through four key design elements that address fundamental limitations of general-purpose LLMs in materials science appli￾cations. First, specialized prompt engineering has proven effective for enhancing domain-specific LLM performance.39,40 Second, the multi-agent architecture enables task decomposi￾tion and specialization, avoiding cognitive overload when single models handle heterogeneous tasks.41,42 Third, structured deci￾sion flows with internal quality checks provide multiple error correction points, ensuring reliable outputs.43 Finally, the knowledge-enhanced mechanism through

hybrid RAG provides professional depth far exceeding general models, enabling scientifically grounded optimization strategies rather than blind trial and error.44,45 Knowledge-driven materials design The design of novel functional materials typically requires re￾searchers to possess extensive cross-disciplinary knowledge and rich experiential accumulation, particularly for complex ma￾terial systems that necessitate balancing multiple performance dimensions. Figure 4 demonstrates in detail how the MARS sys￾tem overcomes limitations of traditional development paradigms to assist scientists in achieving materials design and synthesis validation of perovskite ternary nanocomposite structures (see Note S8). As shown in Figure 4A, traditional materials design cy￾cles typically require several months, encompassing literature review, experimental design, materials synthesis, result valida￾tion,

and experimental optimization. This process heavily de￾pends on researchers’ efforts and experience while simulta￾neously constraining innovation possibilities due to insufficient systematic knowledge integration. In contrast, the MARS-assis￾ted design cycle accelerates this process significantly and en￾ables efficient material design through knowledge-driven and collaborative operations of multiple agents (G1–G5), compress￾ing the entire procedure to just a few hours. While precise wavelength control demonstrates the optimiza￾tion capabilities, the fundamental challenge limiting perovskite nanocrystal applications is their poor stability. Lead halide pe￾rovskites like CsPbBr3 possess ionic crystal structures that readily decompose upon water exposure, causing complete fluorescence quenching within hours. This weakness prevents practical deployment in photovoltaics, LEDs, and other opto

e￾lectrical applications. According to Web of Science analysis (see Figure S7), research on perovskite water stability has grown exponentially, reflecting the urgent need for effective stabiliza￾tion strategies. Given this critical challenge, we tasked MARS with designing water-stable perovskite nanocrystals to show￾case its capability in addressing pressing materials science problems. The multi-round interaction process illustrated in Figure 4B re￾veals how the MARS progresses from mechanistic understand￾ing to creative design through increasingly refined problem anal￾ysis and solution strategies. In round 1, when researchers inquired about core-shell stabilization mechanisms, MARS pro￾vided comprehensive explanations of how this approach pro￾tects perovskites through moisture barriers, defect passivation, thermal stability enhancement, and ion migration suppression. During this explora

tion of stability solutions, researchers noted an additional opportunity revealed by literature analysis: the growing interest in biomedical applications of perovskite mate￾rials (see Figure S8). These applications require both stability and biocompatibility as essential properties. This insight guided the subsequent interaction in round 2, where researchers intro￾duced biocompatibility as an additional requirement. MARS identified this dual challenge and proposed multiple candidate solutions, including oxides, polymers, and biomimetic shells, each with distinct advantages for different application scenarios. From these options, phospholipid encapsulation was ultimately selected by researchers due to two key advantages: the amphi￾philic nature of phospholipids facilitates self-assembly on nano￾crystal surfaces under mild conditions that preserve crystal structure while providing protective encapsulation; and as major components of biological membranes, phospholipids inherently offer excellent biocompatibility. This strategic selection resulted in materials possessing the combined properties of excellent fluorescence, environmental stability, and biocompatibility required for advanced applications in biosensing, cell imaging, and tumor-targeted therapy. When researchers specifically asked about phospholipid bilayer encapsulation in round 3, MARS provided detailed pre￾cursor recommendations including various phospholipids, such as 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DPPC), 1,2-Dioleoyl

-sn-glycero-3-phospho-(1’-rac-glycerol) (DOPG), 1- palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC), 1,2- dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC), and functional components (cholesterol and 1,2-Distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phos￾phorylethanolamine [DSPE]). Following this prioritized recom￾mendation, researchers specified DPPC for further design in round 4. As shown in Figure 4C, MARS identified limited research reports on direct perovskite-DPPC composites through its retrieval results and then analyzed relevant advances in lipo￾somes, quantum dot encapsulation, and biomimetic membrane systems to establish foundations for innovative design. The sys￾tem proposed a ‘‘core-shell-corona’’ ternary structure concept, utilizing a lipid bilayer to provide hydrophobic barriers while intro￾ducing a polyethylene glycol (PEG) corona to enhance colloidal stability. Specifically, the resulting terna

ry structure includes (1) core: CsPbBr3 or MAPbBr3 perovskite nanocrystals, providing excellent optical properties; (2) shell: a liposomal structure composed of DPPC and cholesterol, with cholesterol incorpora￾tion helping to modulate membrane fluidity and mechanical sta￾bility, forming a dense barrier layer that blocks water and oxygen molecule penetration; and (3) corona: DSPE-PEG2000 functional polymer brushes, providing colloidal stability through steric repulsion while conferring biocompatibility and potential for tar￾geted functionalization. Notably, MARS prioritized DPPC in its phospholipid recommendations over the commonly used Figure 4. DOPC in the literature.46–49 The scientific rationale for this recom￾mendation becomes clear when comparing their molecular structures: although both DPPC and DOPC possess neutral phosphocholine headgroups, the saturated palmitic chains (16:0) of DPPC form more densely packed membranes with significantly lower water permeability compared to the unsatu￾rated oleic chains (18:1) of DOPC.50 The incorporation of choles￾terol further enhances membrane organization by promoting liquid-ordered phase formation with DPPC, resulting in an excep￾tionally robust water barrier.51,52 This multi-level structural design achieves synergistic optimization of perovskite surface defect passivation, physical barriers against water/oxygen permeation, and colloidal stability at the molecular level, demonstrating the capability of MARS to integrate multidisciplinary knowledge for creative design. Figure 4D illu

strates the two-step synthesis route designed by MARS, reflecting its professional translation capability from theo￾retical design to experimental protocol (see Note S8). After the re￾searchers acknowledged this design proposal and issued syn￾thesis instructions, MARS generated JSON protocols and automatically performed the synthesis of this composite on our robotic platform. Within 3.5 h of the initial query, perovskite nano￾crystal aqueous solutions were successfully obtained (Figure 4E). To investigate the behavior of CsPbBr3@LP/PEG NCs in an aqueous environment, the evolution of their photoluminescence (PL) was tracked. As detailed in Figure S9A, the PL emission ex￾hibited an initial slow increase followed by a gradual decrease upon water immersion. This fluorescence evolution is not uncom￾mon and has been observed in other phospholipid-coated CsPbX3 systems.53 Previous studies have

demonstrated that in￾teractions with water can lead to surface defect passivation and induce a phase transition from CsPbBr3 to CsPb2Br5, forming heterostructures that initially enhance fluorescence.54,55 Our X-ray crystallography (XRD) characterization confirmed the for￾mation of the CsPb2Br5 phase during water immersion, consis￾tent with these literature reports (see Figure S9B). Cytotoxicity testing confirmed the effectiveness of phospholipid encapsula￾tion in enhancing perovskite biocompatibility. In the evaluation, CsPbBr3@LP/PEG maintained >95% cell viability at concentra￾tions up to 100 μg/mL, while pristine CsPbBr3 showed significant cytotoxicity (see Figure S10). These results demonstrate that phospholipid encapsulation effectively prevents lead ion leaching while improving optical stability for further biological applications. Performance evaluation of the MARS framework The ca

pabilities of MARS were rigorously assessed through pair￾wise win rate based on established LLM evaluation frameworks (see Note S11).56 Specifically, a benchmark dataset comprising 929 materials science text fragments with standardized test questions was constructed through an automated question￾answer pair generation protocol. Claude3.5-Sonnet was em￾ployed to conduct iterative pairwise comparisons between model responses, with randomized response ordering to miti￾gate positional bias.57 This method significantly enhances the measurability of subtle differences between models, ensuring robust discriminative validity and statistical reliability. As shown in Figure 5A, the fundamental architectural advan￾tage of MARS is demonstrated through systematic comparisons using identical base models. When GPT-4o is employed as the foundation in both systems, MARS achieves a 60.02% win rate against

the single-agent implementation. This significant performance reveals critical architectural differences: MARS overcomes the limitations of single-agent systems through hierarchical design, where performance typically degrades when processing extensive contexts and managing multiple simultaneous tasks. By implementing specialized agents with defined responsibilities and enabling multi-round, depth-focused information retrieval within isolated task groups, MARS effec￾tively reduces cognitive burden on individual models while enhancing overall system stability and knowledge integration ca￾pabilities.36 Additionally, MARS also outperforms ChatGPT-4o (the web interface version), achieving a 61.89% win rate. This result demonstrates how domain-specific knowledge integration and hierarchical multi-agent architecture provide advantages over even highly optimized consumer AI systems. Figure 5B

demonstrates the adaptability of MARS across different foundation models, validating the broad applicability of the framework. Beyond the closed-source GPT-4o accessed via API, MARS was successfully implemented using DeepSeek-R1, a powerful open-source model with strong reasoning capabilities. The pairwise comparison results show that MARS (R1) consis￾tently outperforms both the single-agent (R1) and the standalone DeepSeek-R1 model, confirming that the multi-agent architecture provides performance advantages regardless of foundation models. The average win rate analysis in Figure 5C reveals that MARS systems achieve higher overall performance compared to their single-agent counterparts and base models. The overall win rates were calculated by averaging win rates from all unique, non-self pairwise comparisons (see Figure S11). The performance hierarchy clearly shows that MARS benefits fr

om stronger founda￾tion models, with the R1-based implementation achieving higher average win rates than the GPT-4o version. This dependence on base model capabilities suggests that as LLMs continue to improve, the MARS framework will correspondingly enhance its performance in materials science applications. The multi-agent ar￾chitecture thus provides a scalable approach that can adapt to and benefit from ongoing advances in LLMs. While automated benchmarking provides quantitative com￾parisons, validating the practical utility of MARS in domain￾specific scenarios requires expert assessment. Our evaluation panel comprised 10 researchers with extensive expertise in nanomaterial synthesis: 3 PhD candidates, 3 assistant re￾searchers, 2 associate researchers, and 2 professors. All evalu￾ations followed a double-blind protocol, with each test case independently scored by 5 experts. We employed

a 10-point comprehensive scoring system evaluating three primary dimen￾sions: scientific accuracy (40%), task completion (30%), and reasoning quality (30%). The evaluation tasks spanned four key aspects of materials research: structure design, synthesis protocol development, property prediction, and application opti￾mization. Detailed results and task-specific performance ana￾lyses are provided in Note S9, where MARS consistently demon￾strated superior accuracy and experimental actionability compared to baseline models (Figure S12). Having demonstrated the effectiveness of MARS in perov￾skite nanocrystal synthesis, optimization, and design in the Matter 9, 102577, February 4, 2026 9 Article ll

main study, the evaluation was further extended to encompass a broader range of liquid-phase nanomaterial systems. As demonstrated in Figure 5D, MARS was successfully applied to materials across different dimensionalities, including Au nanorods, Ag nanowires, graphene, and black phosphorus nanosheets. For each material system, MARS autonomously designed natural language synthesis protocols, generated structured JSON protocols, and executed experimental pro￾cedures. This comprehensive validation across multiple evaluation methods and diverse material systems, combined with the proven adaptability of the framework to different foun￾dation models, establishes MARS as a broadly applicable plat￾form for accelerating materials research through intelligent automation. DISCUSSION This work introduces MARS, an LLM-driven platform for autono￾mous materials development. MARS integrates 19 specializ

ed agents within a hierarchical framework, which are organized into functional groups to facilitate collaborative execution of complex tasks spanning design, synthesis, and optimization. By leveraging a curated knowledge base and a hybrid RAG approach, MARS achieves enhanced accuracy and mitigates LLM hallucinations, enabling professional-grade, autonomous experimentation. Significantly, MARS achieved rapid optimiza￾tion of material properties (e.g., tuning green-emitting perovskite nanocrystals to blue emission within 10 iterations) and discovery of novel materials within hours, significantly accelerating the Figure 5. research process. Beyond efficiency gains, the MARS architec￾ture enables seamless information flow and knowledge accumu￾lation throughout the research pipeline, creating a responsive closed-loop system that adapts to experimental feedback in real time. MARS represents a significant step toward autonomous mate￾rials research. This system reduces substantial repetitive work, allowing researchers to focus on creative thinking and scientific insights. The flexible, collaborative agent framework permits customization by researchers, enabling integration of local data￾bases and adaptation to diverse experimental platforms. Such features facilitate tailoring to specific research needs while ex￾panding applicability across various materials and synthesis techniques. Despite these advantages, current limitations must be acknowledged. MARS primarily relies on existing literature knowledge for com

binatorial optimization, with its innovative ca￾pacity currently limited to incremental improvements rather than breakthrough discoveries. This reflects fundamental challenges in applying LLMs to scientific research: distinguishing rational inference from hallucinatory outputs and balancing knowledge dependence with exploratory innovation. The system functions as an intelligent research assistant that accelerates discovery cycles rather than replacing human creativity. Beyond performance, reproducibility and runtime error handling represent critical factors for practical adoption in labo￾ratory settings. The MARS architecture addresses reproduc￾ibility through a comprehensive open-source implementation with standardized interfaces between agent modules and ro￾botic components. This design allows other laboratories to repli￾cate system functionality, though some adaptation to specific har

dware configurations remains necessary. Regarding error management, MARS employs a multi-tiered approach to handle failures in both design and synthesis processes: human interven￾tion is strategically integrated at critical decision points, autono￾mous replanning occurs when agents detect suboptimal out￾comes, and rule-based verification protects robotic execution. This flexible error handling capability ensures experimental con￾tinuity despite the unpredictable challenges inherent in materials research, maintaining system reliability without constant expert supervision. Future development will focus on standardized interfaces for laboratory equipment, enabling more complex experimental control. Beyond predefined functions, future LLMs could auton￾omously devise experimental strategies, optimize parameters, and adapt to unexpected situations, realizing embodied intelli￾gence in materials

research. Besides, while the hybrid RAG approach mitigates hallucinations, further advancements in LLM architectures and domain-specific fine-tuning are crucial. Critical directions include integrating physics-based simulations and first-principles calculations to enhance scientific reasoning capabilities, developing more reliable metrics for assessing inno￾vation versus hallucination. We believe the evolution from knowl￾edge-driven to genuinely autonomous innovation represents the necessary trajectory for AI in scientific research, with the current work establishing an important foundation for this long-term goal. Future MARS iterations promise to accelerate materials discovery and development to meet evolving scientific and in￾dustrial demands. METHODS Architecture details MARS design The MARS system utilizes GPT-4o from OpenAI as its foundation model, with the temperature parameter s

et to 0.1 to ensure high stability and consistency during task execution. The AutoGen framework (https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) simplifies complex LLM workflow orchestration, automation, and optimi￾zation through multi-agent dialogue mechanisms. Its flexible ar￾chitecture enables developers to customize agent behaviors and interaction patterns according to specific task requirements. AutoGen provides two core agent types: AssistantAgent and UserProxyAgent. In this study, we utilize AssistantAgent pro￾vided by AutoGen, defining agent roles and functions through system_message and tools parameters. Simultaneously, we set up UserProxyAgent as a human control interface to imple￾ment human-in-the-loop in the multi-agent system, enabling hu￾man intervention at critical points during task execution. In terms of agent orchestration, MARS primarily employs two modes: Selector Group Chat an

d Swarm (https://github.com/openai/ swarm). Selector Group Chat is a multi-agent dialogue mode based on model selection mechanisms, where agents broadcast messages to other members in turns, and an Orchestrator agent selects the next speaking agent or team based on conversation context. The Swarm mode is a multi-agent collaboration mode based on task delegation mechanisms. Agents dynamically delegate tasks to more suitable agents based on task require￾ments and capabilities, ensuring efficient task allocation and execution within the team. The core mechanism of Swarm relies on agents generating HandoffMessages to specify task delega￾tion targets. The admin agents between teams coordinate through the Selector Group Chat mode, while task allocation within teams relies on the Swarm mode. Further details regarding the methods can be found in the supplemental information. SCIENTIST group The

scientist team consists of four materials science agents, each initialized through AssistantAgent. We guide different sci￾entist agents to form different capability preferences through system prompts. Within the scientist team, we use AutoGen’s Swarm mode to orchestrate agents, with four scientist agents communicating directly with the Scientist Team Admin agent through task submission. Knowledge base and retrieval tools We established a knowledge base containing over 100,000 nano-material-related literature papers and developed inter￾faces based on keyword retrieval and vector retrieval for efficient research material access. Specifically, we used the MinerU tool to convert literature PDFs to markdown format for an efficient knowledge base. For the SCIENTIST group, we customized the following retrieval tools. Vector database and search: to opti￾mize the RAG system’s retrieval, we segmen

ted papers by sec￾tion and vectorized text segments using the gte-Qwen2-1.5B￾instruct model (https://huggingface.co/thenlper/gte-large). The vectors are stored in a Weaviate database of Dify, with API func￾tionalized as hybird_retrieval_from_knowledge_base providing KeywordSearch and VectorSearch interfaces based on Matter 9, 102577, February 4, 2026 11 Article ll

keywords and vectors. Knowledge graph: based on the knowl￾edge base, we classified literature by research topics and uti￾lized GraphRAG to construct knowledge graphs for different research topics, with corresponding interfaces available through Autogen Extension. WebSearch and LitSearch: we integrated WebSearch tools based on the Bing search engine and LitSearch tools based on Arxiv and Semantic Scholar for real￾time online searches. Bing searches, arXiv, and Semantic Scholar are called directly through official APIs, which function￾alized as ‘‘paper_retrieval_from_arxiv_and_pubmed’’ and ‘‘onli￾ne_retrieval_with_bing_and_playwright.’’ DatabaseSearch: ma￾terial databases are crucial in nano-materials research. We developed database search tools based on OQMD and Mate￾rials Project (MP) databases, providing comprehensive and pre￾cise material data query capabilities. While the MP database

of￾fers official retrieval interfaces, we simplified and encapsulated their parameters through FastAPI to prevent agent call failures. For the OQMD database, we obtain query results using PlayWright and similarly encapsulate them using FastAPI. ENGINEER group The MARS engineer agent team consists of four agents defined based on AutoGen’s AssistantAgent class, coordinating through system prompts and tools. Within the team, we employ AutoGen’s Swarm mode to organize engineer agents and admin agents, efficiently completing subtasks distributed by the Orches￾trator through task submission. The following tools support the ENGINEER group. Code Sandbox Environment: AutoGen provides DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor, which relies on Docker container isolation environments for code execution that might cause conflicts or crashes in local Python environments. Python REPL: we directly use PythonCodeExe

cutionTool to execute Python code reviewed and confirmed safe by the code reviewer. Object-based storage: we introduced object storage tools using MinIO to build a local object storage service, encapsu￾lated through FastAPI, to maintain the integrity and stability of structured experimental schemes. EXECUTOR group To address potential process blocking during long wait times for characterization data collection, data collection tools are set with a 6-h execution time and a 30-s sleep mechanism when data are unavailable. We customized the following tools for the EXECUTOR group. Mass unit conversion implemented the mol2mg tool based on the periodictable Python package for converting molar mass to weight units. Scheme transmis￾sion API: implemented using FastAPI for transmitting struc￾tured synthesis scheme access links directly to robots or island stations. Results obtain API: implemented u

sing FastAPI for direct access to characterization device data. Camera detector provides IP Camera video stream interface based on RTSP pro￾tocol for real-time monitoring of mobile robots and island stations. Experimental details Cell viability assessment MCF-7 cells were seeded in 96-well plates (1×104 cells/well) and cultured for 24 h. Cells were then incubated with various concen￾trations (0–100 μg/mL) of pristine CsPbBr3 or CsPbBr3@LP/PEG for 24 h. CCK-8 reagent was added, and absorbance was measured at 450 nm. Live/dead staining was performed using the Calcein-AM/PI kit following the manufacturer’s protocol. Viable and dead cell staining MCF-7 cells were incubated in 6-well plates under standard con￾ditions for 24 h. After removal of the digested medium, the cells were treated with fresh medium that contained pristine CsPbBr3 or CsPbBr3@LP/PEG for 4 h of co-culture. Then, cells were

stained with calcein AM (10 μM) and PI (10 μM) according to the product description for 0.5 h. The coloring solution was removed and rinsed twice gently with cold PBS. Finally, the cells were imaged using a fluorescence inverted microscope (Olympus UHGLGPS, China). An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Metamaterial Modeling and Inverse Design Darui Lu,† Jordan M. Malof,‡ and Willie J. Padilla∗,† †Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Duke University, Durham, USA ‡Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Missouri, Columbia, USA E-mail: willie.padilla@duke.edu Abstract The evolution from large language models (LLMs) to agentic systems has created a new frontier of scientific discovery, enabling the automation of complex research tasks that have traditionally required human expertise. We develop and demonstrate such a framework specifically for the inverse design of photonic metamaterials. When queried with a desired optical spectrum, the Agent autonomously proposes and develops a forward deep learning model, accesses external tools via APIs for tasks like optimiza￾tion, utilizes memory, and generates a final

design via a deep inverse method. We demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, highlighting its ability to reason, plan, and adapt its strategy autonomously and in real-time, mirroring the processes of a human researcher. Notably, the Agentic Framework possesses internal reflection and decision flexibility, permitting highly varied and potentially novel outputs. Keywords Artificial intelligence, photonics, metamaterials, metasurfaces, agents, inverse design 1 arXiv:2506.06935v2 [cs.AI] 15 Jul 2025

1 Introduction Deep learning models, such as Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), have shown great promise in photonics research1–3 including metamaterials, 4 metasurfaces,5 plasmonics,6 and photonic crystals.7 One notable application is that of forward modeling where DNNs have been found to accurately predict the properties of metamaterials based upon their design (e.g., geometric properties). Many prior works employ fully connected networks 8–10 and convolutional neu￾ral networks are also a popular choice, particularly for free-form metamaterials. 11–13 Other types of networks have also been explored, including transformers 14–16 and graphical neural networks.17 Another notable application is inverse design, where a DNN is trained to take the desired properties of a metamaterial as input and return the design needed to obtain those properties. A variety of DNN-based inverse design methods have

been proposed such as diffusion models,5 tandem,18 and neural adjoint (NA). 8 We refer the reader to recent reviews (e.g.,19) or tutorials (e.g., 20,21) for a broader discussion of such methods. For both forward and inverse modeling, a human researcher must make numerous design choices: creating an overall plan, choosing simulation tools and settings for dataset gen￾eration, choosing the appropriate machine learning algorithms and their hyperparameters. Once these design choices are made, the resulting process must be implemented in special￾ized software. The design of the algorithms is then typically adjusted iteratively in response to intermediate experimental results. Although these machine learning processes enable the modeling and design of advanced materials, they also require substantial time, which slows scientific progress. The expertise required to set up these procedures also

limits the accessi￾bility of these advanced pipelines. These challenges are not unique to metamaterial research, but extend to scientific computing more broadly, where similar machine learning processes have experienced success (e.g., 22–24). To solve these challenges, we propose to leverage large language model (LLM)-based agentic systems. An agentic framework could replace human decision-making steps in the aforementioned process, dramatically reducing the barrier to adopting advanced machine 2

learning procedures, and relieving human scientists of the time-consuming aspects of the pipeline. In this work, we introduce and validate a novel Agentic Framework capable of performing inverse design of metamaterial photonic systems. The primary contributions of this work are as follows: • We introduce an Agentic Framework that automates the complete end-to-end process of metamaterial inverse design, a scope that includes the autonomous development and optimization of a DNN-based surrogate forward model. • We demonstrate that a system of specialized LLM-based agents can collaborate to achieve similar performance to a human scientist in complex scientific tasks, evincing the power of an agentic approach. • Our framework realizes a novel level of autonomy in scientific research by incorporating internal reflection and dynamic planning, allowing it to adapt its methodology based on interm

ediate results. 2 The Agentic Framework We aim to develop an agentic system to automate an inverse design process that relies upon the Neural Adjoint (NA) inverse method, which is relatively easy to use and has achieved state-of-the-art performance on such modeling tasks. 19,25 We first build an accurate DNN￾based surrogate forward model, which can predict the properties of a metamaterial based upon its design. As discussed, this process of building a DNN-based forward model is now widely-adopted for advanced metamaterial research, and is therefore common practice in modern metamaterial laboratories. The forward modeling process typically consists of two alternating steps: data collection and DNN optimization. During data collection, pairs of designs and metamaterial properties are acquired via experimentation, which is either physical or (more often) numerical simulation. Optimization o

to train and evaluate models. We will often consider multiple DNN model designs and select one that achieves the lowest error on the designated testing data. These two steps of the forward modeling process are repeated – not necessarily in equal proportion – until a suitable level of prediction error is achieved. Once we have an accurate forward model, the NA design method prescribes how we can re-purpose it (i.e., without additional training) to perform inverse design, so that we can simply provide the model with some desired metamaterial properties and it returns a design that will achieve those properties. Here we present an autonomous agent that intelligently engages in the end-to-end metamaterial design process. Our agent replaces the need for manual intervention by dynamically planning and carrying out several complex tasks, which have historically required deep expertise in both p

hotonics and deep learning. To automate the targeted inverse design process, we investigate agentic systems that comprise a collection of large language models (LLMs). LLMs are essentially DNNs that have been trained to take sequences of tokens as input - termed a prompt - and return another sequence of tokens as output. Each token is a numerical vector that can, in principle, represent various types of data such as text, audio, or imagery. In our context, however, a token will usually represent textual characters, and the input and output of the LLM will consist of textual data, such as natural language or and numerical tables. In recent years, LLMs have been shown capable of effectively addressing highly complex prompts, such as answering technical questions about the best machine learning algorithm for a given problem, to carrying out tasks like writing the code to achieve some outcom

e. In more recent research, LLMs have been prompted to use tools to solve tasks or pursue goals, as long as those tools can be manipulated via text (e.g., the LLM can output commands that run a simulator). Despite these powerful emerging capabilities of LLMs, they remain limited in several ways. Although LLMs can exhibit some capability for reasoning, they often struggle with long-term planning of complex multi-step tasks that involve a long sequential set of textual input and output from the LLM. That is they tend to lose sight of the long-term plan while 4

carrying out several tasks, and react more directly to their most recent input prompts. Fur￾thermore LLMs posses a finite-sized context window explicitly limiting their ability to carry out long tasks. Although LLMs can be given access to tools, they might struggle to deter￾mine the correct sequence of tool-use and are poor at handling errors. Some state-of-the-art (SOTA) prompting strategies can offer a degree of mitigation for these limitations, and in￾clude zero / few-shot prompting, 26 system prompting, role prompting, chain of thought, 27 self-consistency,28 and tree of thoughts. 29 However, despite the implementation of SOTA prompting techniques into LLMs, alternative Agentic approaches offer much better perfor￾mance for complex tasks. An Agentic Framework is a system of LLMs and tools working together to carry out complex tasks. By constructing a team of LLMs and giving them acces

s to tools, they may together overcome many of the above listed limitations of LLMs. Although no universal definition exists, a consensus is beginning to emerging, suggesting that an Agentic Framework should be autonomous and goal-oriented, capable of reasoning, planning, and adapting through the use of tools and memory. Our proposed Agentic Framework, depicted in Fig. 1, embodies these principles and pos￾sesses a dedicated planning module (Planner) that orchestrates the overall process including natural language processing (communicating with the user), LLM management, and tool use. Memory in our Agentic Framework is enabled with the OpenAI Agent SDK’s built-in memory store to record and retrieve chat history, permitting the Planner and other LLMs to maintain their effort carrying out tasks and the overarching goal over time. Through the establishment of dedicated LLM modules (blue, yel

low and green blocks) for tool selection and use, reliable and effective results can be achieved, thereby benefiting from the separation of concerns programming concept. 30 The modular approach afforded by our Agentic Frame￾work permits easier development, debugging, and extension to more complex future tasks. Further, typically Agentic frameworks have more, and strategically placed, human-designed system prompts – shown by the red thought bubbles in Fig. 1. The Agentic Framework presented here is not limited to the photonic metamaterial system demonstrated and can be readily extended to other material and spectroscopic systems. 2.1 Planner The Planner Agent gathers essential information from the user to plan the overall research task. During this process the Planner will ask

the user for a target spectrum s ∗ and task details. Specifically, it seeks to understand the task background, primary research objectives, and dataset information. Once the Planner gathers these details, it creates a plan that divides the overall goal into tasks and specifies which agent will handle each. For example, the Planner can decide to: 7

• Develop a forward model • Perform inverse design • Develop both a forward model and perform inverse design The Planner synthesizes a high-level initial strategy which it stores in Memory. We note that this is not a fixed script – the Planner is actively managing each step of the research process and evaluating the results. The outcome of each task is then assessed and the Planner decides the next step that it believes has the best chance for success. The iterative cycle of planning, execution, and analysis of results is what enables our Agentic Framework to adapt its course of action and which may lead to varied and potentially novel results. The Planner Agent additionally generates a detailed task description for AI-Driven Ex￾ploration (AIDE), which is an LLM coding agent for machine learning tasks. 34 This descrip￾tion includes input/output dimensions, evaluation metrics, and possibl

e solutions to ensure controllable code generation. 2.2 Input Verifier The Input Verifier agent ensures that all necessary external files and code inputs required by the process are available and valid. For example, forward modeling requires some means of generating data for model training and validation (e.g., numerical simulation); and inverse design requires a target spectrum file. The input verifier calls the file check tool, which accepts one or more file paths as input, checks their existence, and returns whether each exists. If any of these are missing, the Input Verifier will prompt the user to provide or correct these inputs. 2.3 Forward Modeler The Forward Modeler Agent is designed to develop a deep learning surrogate model via the tool Forward Train shown in Fig. 1. The internal details of the Forward Train tool are 8

presented in Fig. 2. Forward Train consists of an iterative loop that intelligently balances the competing costs of data acquisition (e.g., from numerical simulation) versus model archi￾tecture optimization, which requires training and validation of candidate surrogate models. This entire process is governed by a specialized LLM called the Controller, whose logic is detailed in Algorithm 1. The loop is initialized with an initial dataset of size k0, and a target performance metric Mt . The algorithm uses these inputs to prepare an initial dataset D0 with total size k0, where a training:validation split of 10:1 is used. An initial surrogate model, denoted code0, is automatically generated using AIDE34 (described below), and the performance of this surrogate model is denoted M0. This “initialization” event (k0,M0,Initialization, generate) is recorded in a new history json log H. The contro

ller sets an input target metric Mt as its goal, which will then govern the main iterative loop. At each iteration, the Controller analyzes the performance history (H) and makes a strategic decision. This decision is a hybrid of learned reasoning and hard-coded rules. As governed by its prompt, the Controller is guided to choose progressively larger values for the size of the data set k ′ , to ensure progress. A new dataset D′ containing k ′ samples will be generated (Prepare Dataset in the Algorithm 1). The Controller also outputs an action, a, which can be generate, test, or done. The action test executes Evaluate, which runs the current latest model codelatest on the new dataset and logs its performance M (Evaluate in the Algorithm 1). The action generate invokes AIDE to produce a new model and evaluate it, returning the new code codelatest and its performance M (Code Generation in th

e Algorithm 1). The done action is the LLM’s determination that the process has converged or that the target metric Mt has been reached. The loop also termi￾nates if it hits a hard-coded limit, such as exceeding the maximum data budget or number of rounds (e.g. max rounds = 50; data budget = 50,000 samples), as specified in the algorithm’s termination condition. The Controller also outputs its plain-text reasoning (r) which is a short text description explaining why a particular action was chosen. For each iteration, the 9

Anoop Krishnan 1,3,7 Large language models (LLMs) are transforming laboratory automation by enabling self-driving laboratories (SDLs) that could accelerate materials research. However, current SDL implementations rely on rigid protocols that fail to capture the adaptability and intuition of expert scientists in dynamic experimental settings. Here, we show that LLM agents can automate atomic force microscopy (AFM) through our Artificially Intelligent Lab Assistant (AILA) framework. Further, we develop AFMBench—a comprehensive evalua￾tion suite challenging LLM agents across the complete scientific workflow f

rom experimental design to results analysis. We find that state-of-the-art LLMs struggle with basic tasks and coordination scenarios. Notably, models excel￾ling at materials science question-answering perform poorly in laboratory settings, showing that domain knowledge does not translate to experimental capabilities. Additionally, we observe that LLM agents can deviate from instructions, a phenomenon referred to as sleepwalking, raising safety align￾ment concerns for SDL applications. Our ablations reveal that multi-agent frameworks significantly outperform single-agent approaches, though both remain sensitive to minor changes in instruction formatting or prompting. Finally, we evaluate AILA’s effectiveness in increasingly advanced experiments —AFM calibration, feature detection, mechanical property measurement, graphene layer counting, and indenter detection. These findings establish th

e necessity for benchmarking and robust safety protocols before deploying LLM agents as autonomous laboratory assistants across scientific disciplines. Scientific experimentation demands exceptional domain expertise, from exploration or hypothesis-driven experimental design to preci￾sion execution and rigorous data analysis. This complexity creates bottlenecks in scientific discovery, particularly as experimental tech￾niques grow increasingly sophisticated. The advent of large language models (LLMs) has propelled the development of self-driving laboratories (SDLs) that integrate diverse information sources for automated planning1 and experimentation. Artificial Intelligence (AI)- agents2,3 and SDLs have already achieved several feats in materials or molecular discovery4–6 , chemistry research7 , and inorganic materials synthesis. Additionally, it has been demonstrated that the capability of SDLs can be enhanced by a human-in-the-loop framework that handles disambiguation, thereby enabling better planning and execution11,12. While early demonstrations of LLM-based lab assistants showed promise in chemistry and materials science1–3 , their opera￾tional reliability remains largely uncharacterized beyond specific applications or repetitive use cases with predetermined protocols13–17. Current research predominantly addresses well-documented or predefined protocols and single-objective tasks, failing to capture the intricate interplay between experimental planning, multi-tool coordi￾nation, and result interpretation or online intervention10. While recent investigations

incorporating planning elements have demonstrated success in achieving specific experimental objectives, they have not systematically evaluated SDL reliability across the broader spectrum of laboratory automation tasks13,14. Although several studies have benchmarked LLMs15–23 and vision language models13,14,24,25 through question-answer protocols to assess their potential as materials research co-pilots, a crucial knowledge gap persists: understanding how these AI systems handle novel experimental scenarios and their fundamental limitations. To address this challenge, we here introduce AILA (Artificially Intelligent Lab Assistant), an LLM-powered framework augmented with specialized tools. We selected scanning probe microscopy18, specifically atomic force microscopy (AFM), as our experimental testbed, given its inherent complexity and broad applicability in materials research. There have

been several efforts to automate microscopy techniques using AI and human-in-the-loop approaches due to their extensive applications in materials characterization26–35. These efforts focus exclusively on advancing specific operational aspects, such as analysing moving objects or optimizing illumination conditions, with an emphasis on improving individual steps within the broader experimental protocol. In addition to these targeted advancements, Liu et al.36 explores the integration of LLMs with Application Programming Interface (API) to enhance workflow pre￾paration, instrument operation, and data reproducibility in scanning probe microscopy research. AFM operation demands expertise across multiple domains—from probe calibration to parameter optimization and data interpretation—making it an ideal platform for evaluating AI agents’ ability to manage sophisticated experimental workflows.

Using AFM as the model system, we probe AILA’s capabilities through AFMBench on five critical aspects of scientific automation: experimental workflow design, multi-tool coordination, decision￾making, execution of open-ended experiments, and data analysis. Our systematic evaluation reveals key failure modes and areas requiring enhancement. We demonstrate AILA’s practical utility through five real-world experiments: (1) identification and analysis of an indenta￾tion mark on a glass sample, including inference of the indenter type used; (2) detection of graphene flakes on a silicon wafer and deter￾mination of the number of graphene layers present; (3) automated microscope calibration; (4) high-resolution imaging of graphene step edges; and (5) load-dependent friction characterization on highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG). Results AILA framework AILA’s architecture prioritizes modular

ity, enabling seamless integra￾tion with diverse experimental and analytical platforms. At its core lies an LLM-powered planner—the framework’s cognitive centre—which orchestrates user interactions and coordinates specialized agents (Fig. 1a). This planner directly takes query from a user and identifies the appropriate agent to handle the task. The agent makes tool calls to carry out the necessary steps to complete the experiment. The agent￾to-agent coordination is invoked by two keywords, namely, “NEED HELP” and “FINAL ANSWER”. While the former flag invokes a routing function that transfers the unresolved task to the next appropriate agent, the latter flag results in the termination of the experiment. Thus, AILA employs a dynamic routing, exploiting available agents and tools, for completing the task given by the user (see S2.4 in Supplementary Information for additional details). For A

FM operations, AILA deploys two agents: the AFM Handler Agent (AFM-HA) for experimental control and the Data Handler Agent (DHA) for analysis. The AFM-HA interfaces with a document retrieval system comprising AFM software documentation and a code execu￾tion engine that translates Python commands into experimental actions. A Python-based API establishes the hardware-software inter￾face, enabling direct control of the AFM system through vendor￾specific protocols (Fig. 1b). The DHA manages image optimization and analysis through dedicated tools: an Image Optimizer that fine-tunes Proportional-integral-derivative (PID) parameters for high-fidelity imaging and an Image Analyzer that extracts targeted features from experimental data. For queries beyond agent capabilities, the planner generates alternative approaches or recommended actions. In an AFM experiment, the workflow usually involves tw

o key steps: capturing the image and analysing the results. The imaging part starts with choosing the right cantilever, then setting the imaging parameters. Afterwards, the tip is gently moved toward the sample surface, and the scan is carried out. For every stage, AILA creates a specific Python script and executes it, controlling the AFM instrument in real-time through an API. This connection allows the digital com￾mands to directly translate into physical movements on the instru￾ment. Once the scan is complete, the image is saved automatically and opened for analysis. The technical specifications and implementation details of each module are explained in the Methodology section. To demonstrate AILA’s operational workflow, we present a multi￾step experiment: acquiring an AFM image of HOPG and extracting its friction and roughness parameters (Fig. 1c). This open-ended task exemplifies re

al-world complexity, offering multiple solution path￾ways. Upon receiving the query, AILA dissects it into sequential objectives: image acquisition via AFM-HA followed by DHA-led analy￾sis. AFM-HA retrieves relevant documentation, generates executable code, and captures the image. Following successful acquisition, AILA transitions control to DHA, which directs the Image Analyzer to com￾pute the specified parameters. This orchestrated sequence exemplifies AILA’s core strengths: the ability to parse complex natural language queries, develop strategic workflows, and coordinate multiple agents toward achieving experimental objectives. AFMBench: tasks for evaluating the AILA framework AFMBench comprises 100 expertly curated experimental tasks (see S3.1 in Supplementary Information for a few examples of tasks; all the tasks are available in the GitHub repo37), manually designed to rigor￾ously

evaluate autonomous AFM operations across multiple dimen￾sions of complexity. Unlike conventional LLM benchmarks or simulation-based evaluations, AFMBench task demands physical execution on AFM hardware, introducing real-world temporal con￾straints and experimental variability. Analysis of the tasks reveal dis￾tinct patterns in resource utilization and operational complexity. In Fig. 2a, tool coordination requirements highlight a systematic pre￾ference for sophisticated workflows, with 69% of tasks demanding multi-tool integration, while 31% operate through single-tool proto￾cols. Agent deployment analysis reveals a distribution: 83% of opera￾tions utilize single-agent protocols, while 17% require multi-agent coordination—enabling evaluation of both targeted expertise and system-wide integration capabilities. In Fig. 2b, the operational landscape is divided into two primary complexity ti

ers: basic operations (56%) encompassing fundamental microscopy tasks and advanced procedures (44%) requiring more sophisticated experimental workflows (for example questions see Article https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64105-7 Nature Communications | (2025) 16:9104 2

Fig. 2e). Core system components—the AFM Handler, Document Retriever tool, and Code Executor tool—demonstrate maximum engagement, each activating in 66 distinct tasks (see Fig. 2c). The Data Handler Agent and Image Analyzer tool exhibit selective activation patterns (52 and 48 tasks, respectively), while the Image Optimizer tool engages exclusively in critical parameter optimization scenarios (4 tasks). Task distribution across functional domains reveals three primary clusters: documentation (50 standalone tasks), analysis (14 tasks), and calculation (10 tasks) (see Fig. 2d). A significant overlap between these domains emerges through integrated tasks that combine multiple functional requirements, reflecting the interconnected nature of experimental workflows. This carefully constructed distribution enables systematic evaluation of AI systems across a spectrum of experimental complexity—

Safety alignment in SDLs To understand the safety challenges39 of AI agents, we evaluate the effectiveness of implementing a safety framework in AILA. First, we establish restricted access protocols for critical AFM functions, coupled with ethical system prompts (see S2.1 in Supplementary Information) that constrain code generation to predefined documentation40. To implement this, we classified all the operations that could be performed on an AFM as per the instrument’s doc￾umentation into two categories. (i) General operations—these include setting imaging parameters, controlling the tip, selecting the scanning area, and other standard tasks. (ii) Critical

operations— these involve sensitive adjustments such as factory calibrations, laser alignment, piezo calibration, and thermal calibration. Even a minor coding error in critical operations could seriously damage the instrument. We restricted the access to the documentation of critical operations in AILA, while allowing complete access to the doc￾umentation of general operations. The critical functions are limited to trained human experts. Note that general operations were selected in such a fashion that any experiment that could potentially be performed on an AFM could be carried out using some combi￾nation of these operations. Thus, the predefined documentation in AILA does not restrict any new experiment to be performed on the AFM instrument. Note that an alternate approach to implement safety is to identify risky actions and involve a human-in-the-loop mechanism to review the actions.

This could also enhance the robustness and overall performance of the framework. However, such a framework requires human supervision, limiting the high￾throughput nature that an autonomous system can otherwise achieve, with human response becoming the bottleneck. Hence, this approach was not implemented in AILA and could be explored as part of future work. Second, we develop strict operational boundaries that permit dynamic code generation solely for image analysis while preventing external software installation or system modifications. Evaluation of the improved protocol demonstrates the effectiveness of these safe￾guards—AILA appropriately failed when prompted to install external Python libraries. (see S3.3 in Supplementary Information for complete validation logs). These findings underscore the critical importance of robust safety protocols in SDLs, emphasizing the necessity of com￾p

rehensive benchmarking and operational guardrails.
